label: Chapter 7
title: The page becomes blocks
dek: On 6 December 2018 the editing screen a generation of writers knew was replaced. What changed underneath mattered more than what changed on top.

blocks.text: For fifteen years a WordPress post was one long field of text. Anything more elaborate — a gallery, a form — was done with shortcodes: bracketed instructions such as `[gallery]`, typed on trust and seen only after publishing.

blocks: In January 2017 Matías Ventura, leading the editor work with Joen Asmussen, named the problem: content in WordPress “has no inherent data structure.”[^focus-leads][^editor-overview] The answer was to treat each paragraph, image and heading as a *block* — a unit the software can recognise — while still saving the post as ordinary HTML. By February the project had a name: Gutenberg.[^gutenberg-prototype]

blocks.caption: The editing screen before and after WordPress 5.0, redrawn and simplified. The comment syntax at the bottom is the real one.

steps.label: Before
steps.text: The classic editor: a title and one box. Heading, paragraphs and picture all live in the same stream of text, and the software cannot tell where one ends and the next begins.

steps.label: 6 December 2018
steps.text: WordPress 5.0 opens the same article and shows its seams. The writing has not changed. Each part is now a block that can be selected, moved or replaced on its own.[^wp50]

steps.label: Underneath
steps.text: What is saved is still HTML. Each block is marked off by a comment that browsers ignore. “Honoring the user content as HTML is important,” Ventura wrote: it “avoids platform lock-in.”[^theseus]

blocks.text: A release that pleased and alarmed the same people

blocks: Getting there was rough. A licensing dispute over Facebook’s React library nearly forced a rewrite in 2017.[^react][^fb-relicense] The release date slipped twice, then was fixed with about two days’ notice, on the eve of WordCamp US, the project’s flagship American conference.[^new-date]

Reactions did not sort neatly into for and against. Joost de Valk of Yoast wrote “I love Gutenberg” in the very post that asked for a delay.[^devalk-2018] Rian Rietveld resigned as head of the accessibility team, which then said it could not, as things stood, recommend the editor to people who rely on assistive technology.[^rietveld][^a11y-report] An independent audit in 2019 found “significant and pervasive accessibility problems” — and, for the most part, clean and accessible output.[^audit-summary]

A plugin restoring the old editor has sat on millions of sites ever since,[^classic-editor] and a fork, ClassicPress, was started in protest.[^classicpress] Accessibility fixes followed in later releases.[^wp53] Two days after 5.0, Mullenweg described the editor as a first phase and revealed a third and fourth to come.[^phases]

blocks.title: The accessibility record, in its own words

items.text: To Matt Mullenweg I want to say: please take better care of your community, because WordPress is nothing without it.
These problems are solvable. Retrofitting accessibility is not an effective process.
We did kind of have some project management fails in this process where we had a team of volunteers that felt like they were disconnected from the rapid development that was happening with Gutenberg.
items.where: WordCamp Portland, as transcribed by WP Tavern

rows: Commissioned by WPCampus, a higher-education community; carried out by Tenon; cost just under $31,200, of which more than 100 community members gave $10,264 and Matt Mullenweg and Automattic covered the balance.[^audit-vendor][^audit]

90 issues; an average task completion rate of 63% among nine testers; and, in the editor’s favour: “For the most part, the markup generated from the Gutenberg editor is clean, semantically correct and accessible.”[^audit-summary]
WPCampus asked that it be read as “a snapshot of the state of the editor in early 2019.” By publication, 116 further accessibility issues had been closed.[^audit]
In December 2019 Rietveld added to her post that “other people have stepped up and there have been made improvements.”[^rietveld]

blocks.title: Stars, installs and a referendum of sorts

rows: The Gutenberg plugin averaged 2.7 stars out of 5 at the start of August 2018 and 2.3 by the end of that month, where it still stood the day after 5.0 shipped.[^tavern-200k][^gutenberg-rating]

Shown as 600,000+ active installs on 7 December 2018, 5+ million from mid-2019, 10+ million in mid-2024, and 8+ million on 30 September 2026. These are rounded-down bands, so they blur real movement.[^classic-editor]
“Until December 31, 2021” at first; today, “until 2024, or as long as is necessary.”[^classic-window][^classic-editor]
By late 2019, per Jetpack’s statistics, more than 50 million posts had been written in the block editor — a partial sample, reported at State of the Word.[^sotw-2019]

items.text: I welcome it; apathy would worry me a lot more than disagreement or controversy.
items.where: “We Called it Gutenberg for a Reason”

items.text: The 5.0 announcement itself carried a caution: “Note to users of assistive technology: if you experience usability issues with the block editor, we recommend you continue to use the Classic Editor.”[^wp50]
